source.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
source.authors: Cheng-Yu Xie; Fei Shen; Shu-Yi Miao; Yue Feng; Jian Yu; Pengyang Shao; Yi-Jun Tian; Xiao-Yu Du

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and table layout show formatting/encoding artifacts, but the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper treats FFN output coordinates as neuron-level targets and uses them for safety interventions and fine-tuning. It does not test whether neurons have one or two interpretable jobs, validate explanations on held-out activations, or build attribution graphs as in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron suppression and activation-state transfer results, recorded below as related findings with versions ["none"]. Its SK-Masked LoRA and benchmark-comparison results concern the performance of its proposed safety method, not the interpretability or explanation claims, and are not recorded as rows. The paper's background claims about other studies are not its own results.
record.test_reason: The paper treats FFN output coordinates as intervention units for multilingual safety. It never audits how many neurons have one or two interpretable jobs, never checks neuron explanations against held-out activations, and builds no attribution graphs. Its suppression and activation-transfer results measure refusal ASR, not neuron interpretability, so no claim version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a compact, cross-lingually shared set of FFN output coordinates (the safety kernel) is functionally associated with multilingual safety: suppressing it weakens refusal, and injecting a safe-refusal state strengthens it. SK-Masked LoRA cuts ASR, including on languages excluded from SK discovery, with limited capability cost. ASR is judged by GPT-4o.
record.recipe_differences: The study identifies safety-related FFN output coordinates using SCAR and tests them through suppression and activation-state transfer; it does not use the original claim's neuron-pole job audit or explanation-testing recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies discovery-language composition and top-k for its safety-neuron method; it reports top-k effects on suppression and SK-size changes when languages are excluded. These are method sensitivities, not interpretability-audit outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Suppressing the top-5000 SCAR-ranked FFN output coordinates per language raises MultiJail ASR to about 70–81% in Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Size-matched random masks leave average ASR near default. The intersection set (SK, 0.12–0.15% of coordinates) keeps about 90% of that effect. Injecting a safe-refusal SK activation state lowers average ASR in all three models (20.21→11.96, 35.98→30.69, 5.18→3.17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A small set of FFN output coordinates shared across languages is causally associated with refusal of harmful requests across languages, as measured by suppression and activation-transfer interventions.

record.problems: The reported intervention results do not measure neuron interpretability or explanation validity. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the reported ASR results; the activation-transfer results are summarized as averages across target languages in the text, with Figure 3 providing the language-specific display.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded SK-Masked LoRA training results and method comparisons in Tables 3–5, as they report the performance of the paper's proposed safety-training method rather than test any claim version about neuron interpretability or explanation validity. Also excluded the Top-k sweep and discovery-language sensitivity results because they tune or characterize the proposed selection method, not the claim versions.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles and no shares of single-job, two-job or unexplained neurons.
No interpretability shares for any model; the three 8–9B models are used only for safety interventions.
No vision models and no analysis of canonical polysemantic neurons or superposition.
No comparison of interpretability rates across architectures, regularization or tools.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
No neuron explanations and no test of predicting firing on held-out text.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Here 'neuron' means an FFN output activation coordinate, picked by SCAR contrast statistics rather than by interpreting it. No study result bears on neuron interpretability shares, explanation validity or attribution graphs. The paper does not cite the original essay. Per-language random-mask controls vary by up to about 20 points (Llama BN, KO) and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report proportions with one job, two related jobs, or jobs not understood.
Tests safety-related coordinates in three models, not whether the claimed interpretability shares hold across models, architectures, or scale.
Does not analyze InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or test recursive generalization against superposition.
Does not test whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain interpretability rates, or estimate rates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on new examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
